notes:
I've put these notes together verse by verse below. I read the full Enduring Word (Guzik), Constable (StudyLight) and NET Bible pages. The other sources (Matthew Henry, Gill, Clarke, Coffman, Pett, JFB, Ellicott, Keil & Delitzsch, Precept Austin, Bible Odyssey, GotQuestions and TGC) come from search excerpts only, so I didn't see their full commentary.

**Gaps in what I found:**
- I found nothing on the Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org).
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter.
- I couldn't open the Pulpit Commentary, the full Gill text, or the Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) and Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) sites.
- I found no clear split between denominations on this chapter. The real disagreements cut across traditions. I've marked them **[Debated]**.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** "No king" means more than a missing ruler. It signals that Israel refused to recognize God's leadership over them. F.B. Meyer even advised readers to stop after this verse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- Guzik says the concubine was recognized as his legal partner, but she did not have the same status in the home or in society as a wife. He adds that from the beginning God's plan was one man and one woman to be one flesh forever (Matthew 19:4-6). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-19.cfm
- **[Debated] Was taking a concubine wrong?**
  - **Constable:** Since monogamy was God's standard for marriage the Levite should not have married a concubine (Genesis 2:24). This was doubly wrong in the case of a Levite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
  - **TGC (Carson, Reformed site):** Levites were supposed to marry only virgins; see Lev. 21:7, 13-15. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/judges-19-acts-23-jeremiah-33-psalms-3-4/
  - **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes the milder view:** It was no disreputable connection this Levite had formed; for a nuptial engagement with a concubine wife ... possessed the true essence of marriage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_019.cfm
  - **Ellicott takes a middle view:** such connections were not legally forbidden; yet it is probable that in the case of all but princes or eminent men they were looked on with moral disapprobation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/19-1.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** she was called a concubine because she was not endowed, but it doesn't appear he had another wife. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC07019.HTM
- **Gill:** the Levite may have lived there to be near the tabernacle at Shiloh. Bethlehem's shame from this story was wiped off by the birth of some eminent persons in it, as Boaz, Jesse, David, and especially the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/19-1.htm

**v. 2** **[Debated] Did she commit adultery, or did she leave in anger?**
- **NET note:** the verb may not come from "to be a prostitute" at all. It may be derived from a root meaning "to be angry; to hate" attested in Akkadian. NET's own translation reads "got angry at him." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Matthew Henry** reads it as adultery. He notes that the Chaldee reads it only that she carried herself insolently to him, or despised him. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC07019.HTM
- **Cundall (quoted by Constable)** prefers "angry": the penalty against the adulteress was death (Leviticus 20:10), but a heated argument would allow the Levite to seek a reconciliation. Constable himself sides with the Hebrew text ("unfaithful"). He also suggests the four-month wait shows the Levite wasn't eager to get her back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** sees a problem with the adultery reading: it rendered it unlawful for her husband to take her back ( Deu 24:4 ). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_019.cfm
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, Susanne Scholz):** reverses the reading. The girl escapes to her father's house after being statutorily raped by the Levite man. https://concordiatheology.bibleodyssey.org/articles/concubine/

**v. 3**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** here the Levite is an example of how an offended spouse should act when there is adultery. Though she broke the bond between them, he worked hard to bring the relationship back together. He links this to Jesus' teaching that divorce is never *commanded* after adultery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **Matthew Henry:** that she wasn't prosecuted was a sign there was no king, no judge, in Israel, else she would have been prosecuted and put to death as an adulteress. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC07019.HTM
- **Constable, more sceptical:** The Levite's tender words were insincere, as his later dealings with her prove. Apparently he wanted her back for selfish reasons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Coffman:** the phrase "speak kindly" suggests the Levite himself was to blame for the break-up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/19-2.html
- **NET note:** the Hebrew is literally "to speak to her heart." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **On the father's welcome:** Guzik offers two options. Perhaps the father was glad to see the Levite and his daughter back together or perhaps the father was simply glad to have his daughter out of his house again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-19.cfm

**vv. 4–9**
- **Guzik:** these verses explain the delay. The long stay is why they left late in the day instead of early in the morning. https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_jdg/jdg_19.cfm
- **Constable:** the father-in-law is the most admirable person in the chapter, because he showed love to both the man and the woman. His hospitality sets up a contrast with Gibeah. Constable also notes that the hospitable host lived in Bethlehem, David's town, while Saul came from Gibeah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Coffman:** the parents probably expected not to see her for a long time. The Levite should have stayed another night, as it was very bad judgment on his part to leave in the middle of the afternoon. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/judges-19.html#1-30
- **v. 6 (Precept Austin):** some translations say "the two men" ate, so presumably the concubine was not present during the meals. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_19_commentary

**v. 10**
- **Constable:** Jebus (Jerusalem) was and is about six miles north of Bethlehem (Judges 19:10). The Levite and his concubine would have reached it in about two hours. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **NET note:** some ancient witnesses add "and his servant" to the list of who was with him. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19

**vv. 11–13**
- **Guzik:** The Levite and his concubine considered a pagan town too dangerous. They therefore went on to Gibeah, a city of Israel, because they thought they would be safer there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **Matthew Henry** approves of the choice. By avoiding Jebus he would witness against the wickedness of those that contracted friendship and familiarity with these devoted nations. Let Israelites, Levites especially, associate with Israelites. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC07019.HTM
- **Constable sees irony:** The Levite expected to find hate in Jebus and love in Gibeah. He would have been wiser to stop for the night in Jebus. Gibeah was three miles further on, and Ramah two beyond that. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/19-2.html
- **Pett:** The Levite was a patriotic and religious man and preferred not to depend on or trust foreigners if he could help it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-19.html

**vv. 14–15**
- **Guzik:** the lack of welcome reflects poorly on the people of Gibeah because God commanded such hospitality among the people of God (Leviticus 19:33-34, Leviticus 25:35, Matthew 25:35, Hebrews 13:2). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-19.cfm
- **Constable, quoting Block:** this refusal would have shocked anyone in the ancient Near East, all the more because the travellers were fellow Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html

**vv. 16–17**
- **Guzik:** The only person to extend hospitality to the Levite and his concubine was a man from their own region. None of the native people of Gibeah cared for the strangers in their midst. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **Matthew Henry:** Though there as not one of Gibeah, yet it proved there was one in Gibeah who showed kindness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/judges/19.htm

**v. 18**
- **Guzik:** The house of the LORD was not at Jerusalem, but at Shiloh (Judges 18:31). https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_jdg/jdg_19.cfm
- **NET note:** the "house of the LORD" might refer to the shrine at Shiloh. The LXX reads "to my house." NET translates "heading home." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Matthew Henry:** Gibeah may have refused him *because* he was going to the house of the Lord. The old man was kinder for that same reason, receiving a servant of God for his Master's sake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/judges/19.htm
- **Coffman goes further,** calling it clear that the men of Gibeah refused him because of his faith in God and his connection with the house of Jehovah at Shiloh. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/judges-19.html#1-30

**v. 19**
- **NET note:** By calling his concubine the old man's "female servant," the Levite emphasizes their dependence on him for shelter. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Constable:** Judges 19:19 shows that there was no reason for the Gibeahites to refuse the Levite hospitality. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html

**vv. 20–21**
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** sleeping outdoors wasn't unusual in the East, so the old man's warning arose from his acquaintance with the infamous practices of the place. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_019.cfm
- **Constable:** from v. 21 on, the story sounds like Lot in Sodom replayed. Gibeah proved to be New Sodom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html

**v. 22**
- **Guzik:** the demand echoes the men of Sodom (Genesis 19:5). The verb form for "beat on the door" shows an increasingly loud pounding. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **NET note:** "Good-for-nothings" is literally "sons of wickedness." Judges 20:5 implicates the town leaders. If so, the implication is that the entire male population of the town were good-for-nothings. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Carson (TGC):** refusing hospitality was unthinkable in that culture, and the mob will happily rape males or females — they don't really care. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/judges-19-acts-23-jeremiah-33-psalms-3-4/
- **Matthew Henry** cites Josephus, who makes her to be the person they had a design upon when they beset the house, and says nothing of their villainous design upon the Levite himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/judges/19.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- **Carson (TGC)** calls this perhaps the ugliest moment in the story. The host, remembering the rules of hospitality and doubtless frightened for himself as well, offers them his daughter and the Levite's concubine. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/judges-19-acts-23-jeremiah-33-psalms-3-4/
- **Constable:** "Do to them whatever you please" is literally "what is good in your eyes," the book's refrain. "Do to them ... whatever you please [i.e., what is right in your own eyes]." And they did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** The host's offer shows distorted ethics shaped by cultural pressure. Scripture records it but does not endorse it. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/judges/19.htm
- **Coffman** links this to how little women were valued then, citing Abraham and Sarah. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/judges-19.html#1-30

**v. 25** **[Debated] How guilty was the Levite?**
- **The majority view across traditions is severe:**
  - **Guzik:** the Levite and the host were guilty too. They clearly should have been willing to sacrifice themselves rather than give up the women. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
  - **Constable:** the Levite was more guilty than the old stranger because he sacrificed his concubine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
  - **Precept Austin:** the Hebrew verb (*chazaq*) means he took her by force. This is unimaginable weakness and cowardice for a husband. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_19_commentary
  - **Clarke (Methodist):** the mob, the Levite and the old man are all characters that humanity and modesty wish to be buried in everlasting oblivion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/19-25.html
- **Softer readings:**
  - **Gill:** the Levite put her out very probably with her consent, to try if that would pacify them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/19-25.html
  - **Pett** is unusually sympathetic. He speculates that she may well have been a cult prostitute, and argues that he certainly expected her to be alive in the morning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-19.html
- **[Debated] Was her death a judgment on her?**
  - **Matthew Henry says yes:** In the miserable end of this woman, we may see the righteous hand of God punishing her for her former uncleanness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_019.cfm
  - **Guzik says the opposite:** everyone was guilty except of course for the concubine herself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, Graybill):** the rape of the concubine is framed as a harm done to her husband, not to the woman herself, even as she ends up dead. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-levites-concubine/

**v. 26**
- **NET note:** the word "master" here is plural in Hebrew. The plural indicates degree here and emphasizes the Levite's absolute sovereignty over the woman. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Constable:** perhaps the writer says "master" instead of "husband" because the Levite treated her as property. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html

**vv. 27–28**
- **Guzik:** "Get up" is a painfully clear demonstration of the heartlessness of the Levite towards his concubine. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-19.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** he seems to have had a good night's sleep. To him she was little more than chattel ... when in fact she was a being created in the image of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_19_commentary
- **Constable, quoting McCann:** Achsah on a donkey (1:14) and this woman on a donkey bracket the whole book. This tracks a decline marked by increasing violence against women. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **[Debated] Was she already dead?**
  - **Bible.org:** the text does not exactly tell us that she was already dead, it does inform us that she was not responsive. https://bible.org/seriespage/17-israel-s-sodom-and-gomorrah-judges-19-21
  - **Matthew Henry** suggests the Levite didn't follow her out because he was afraid of being harmed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_019.cfm

**v. 29**
- **Guzik:** This was an obviously grotesque way to deliver a message, but the method worked. It was tragic that the Levite did not show this kind of concern for righteousness earlier. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/judges/judges-19.cfm
- **Constable:** he cut her up the way one would slaughter an animal. He later described what happened as though she was already dead when he cut her up (Judges 20:5-6), but we wonder if we can believe him. He may have killed her himself. Constable also compares Saul's summons using an animal in 1 Samuel 11:7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Precept Austin:** he sought revenge on a national scale, but we see no sign of self-judgment on his own part. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_19_commentary
- **Matthew Henry:** he wanted to show how barbarously she had been treated, and to stir up the same passionate concern in others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/19-25.html
- **Bible Hub study notes:** in ancient context it was a call to arms when time was critical. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/judges/19.htm
- **Coffman:** the war that followed was not for the purpose of avenging the death of the innocent and helpless concubine, but to avenge the trespass of the husband's property rights! and to punish Gibeah for the violation of the laws of hospitality. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/judges-19.html#1-30

**v. 30**
- **Pett:** It was a call for action and judgment in legal jargon. They were to weigh up the situation, discuss the matter together and then come to a decision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-19.html
- **NET note:** Codex Alexandrinus of the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) adds lines in which the Levite tells his messengers what to say to every Israelite. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Jdg&chapter=19
- **Guzik:** Israel remembered this crime for centuries (Hosea 9:9 and 10:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-19/
- **Constable:** the real question is whether Israel will now follow God's law. Quoting Block, he notes that this nameless Levite rallied the whole nation in a way no judge had. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-19.html
- **Pointing to Christ:**
  - **GotQuestions:** this period would soon lead to the demand for an Israelite king ... yet would also reveal the need for a perfect King and Messiah—Jesus Christ. https://www.gotquestions.org/Levite-concubine.html
  - **Carson (TGC)** reads the Levite's message as asking when the violence will stop. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/judges-19-acts-23-jeremiah-33-psalms-3-4/
